lesson.menu_title: The Listening Gap — Why Americans Sound So Fast
lesson.menu_desc: The sounds English eats, and the four sentences that buy you time -- 36 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 4 -- The Listening Gap
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Braulio Zemel | Lesson 4 -- The Listening Gap
lesson.grammar_point: wish + past simple and wish + past perfect

listenings.text: Good evening everyone, and thanks for coming out. Just a few quick things before we start. The talk tonight runs about fifty minutes and we will take questions for fifteen after that, so we should all be out by nine. If you signed up for the reading group, we have moved it from Wednesday to Thursday, same time, same room, starting next week. There are still four places. Coffee is at the back and it is free tonight. And if anyone finds a grey umbrella, it belongs to the gentleman in the second row, and he has already asked me twice.

Here is a drill you can do in four minutes a day, and it is more useful than any app. Take one minute of audio, anything with a transcript, and listen to it three times. The first time, do not read, and do not try to catch every word. Write down only the words you are certain about, even if there are five of them. The second time, still without the text, fill in what you can around those five. Only on the third pass do you open the transcript, and when you do, look for the gaps you left and ask what happened in them. You will find the same two or three things happening over and over. Learn those, and the speed problem quietly becomes a smaller problem.

extra_audio.text: Grace tells Braulio that his question at the end was a good one, because most people just nod for an hour and leave. He admits that he lost the thread in the middle, when the speaker started on the figures. Grace says she lost it as well, because the speaker went twice as fast for two slides. Braulio asks her what people actually say when they miss a piece. She tells him to say could you rephrase that, because repeating the same words rarely helps.

reading.rtitle: The Sounds That Are Not There
paras: Learners almost always describe the problem as speed, and almost always they are describing something else. Fast speech in English is not the same sentence played faster. It is a different sentence, with material removed.

Three things happen. Words link, so that the end of one runs into the beginning of the next and did you eat arrives as a single block. Sounds weaken, so that the vowel in for and to and of collapses into a soft, colourless sound that carries no information at all. And whole consonants disappear, so that next day loses its t and I don't know becomes something closer to a hum with three notes in it.

None of this is careless, and none of it is rude. It is what every native speaker does, including the ones who believe they speak clearly, and including the newsreaders. A speaker who genuinely pronounced every sound in every word would sound strange and slightly threatening.

There is one piece of good news in this, and it is bigger than it looks. What disappears is almost never the information. English protects the words that matter and eats the ones that do not, which means a listener who catches only the strong syllables has usually caught the message. If you have been trying to hear everything, you have been trying to do something that native listeners do not do either.
reading.source: Article -- The Sound of English, a language newsletter
